Even so, efforts to reduce food insecurity have regressed since the 2010s: severe food insecurity affected 9.5 percent of the global population in 2025, compared with an average of 8.1 percent in 2015–19 (figure 6.B). Moreover, the baseline outlook brings an end to the tailwind from falling global food commodity prices between 2023 and 2025, which had put downward pressure on consumer food costs. In this context, EMDE food price inflation picked up to a median of 3.9 percent (y/y) in 2026Q3, from 3.5 percent the previous quarter, and may firm further as sizable increases in grain and oilseed prices feed through.

The number of people experiencing severe food insecurity worldwide fell to about 779 million in 2025 from 803 million in 2024 and 837 million in 2021 (figure 15.B). The 21 percent decline in global food commodity prices between 2022 and 2025 likely contributed to these gains. Even so, severe food insecurity affected 9.5 percent of the global population in 2025, well above the 8.1 percent average in the five years before COVID-19. With food prices forecast to rise by a cumulative 18 percent in 2026–27 amid overlapping weather, logistics, and conflict shocks, this tailwind for the fight against hunger appears set to become a headwind. events.query: very strong El Niño episodes since 1950

results.text: Episodes of El Niño vary considerably in intensity (figure B1.2.A).a Since 1950, there have been 27 El Niño episodes, four of which were very strong (in 1982–83, 1991–92, 1997–98, and 2015–16), with the current episode expected to become the fifth. Over the same period, there were 3 strong, 9 moderate, and 11 weak episodes. El Niño episodes typically emerge around May or June, strengthen through the third quarter of the year, peak near year-end, and dissipate during the first half of the following year. As a result, much of the associated rainfall anomaly occurs during the second half of the year, overlapping with the growing season for several major internationally traded commodities.

Episodes vary widely in intensity, and only a minority—eight out of 26 episodes since 1950—have been classified as strong or very strong.6 Commodity prices are higher during ENSO episodes than during neutral periods (box 1). However, price sensitivity differs from volatility transmission: a large movement in a commodity’s own price does not necessarily make it a stronger source of volatility for other markets. The results indicate that the strong phase of the 2015-16 El Niño was associated with much larger increases in transmitted connectedness than the weak phase (figure SF .4.B). Soybeans recorded the largest increase in connectedness during the strong phase, followed by maize. During the weak phase, maize transmission was broadly unchanged, while the increase for soybeans was similar to that for non-food commodities.

The agency also estimates an 83 percent chance that it will become the strongest El Niño since 1950 (when comparable records begin) during October–De- cember 2026 (figure 13.A).2 El Niño typically brings drier conditions to parts of Australia, Central America, the Sahel, South and Southeast Asia, and Southern Africa, and wetter conditions to parts of Central Asia, China, and the southern United States. Its effects on East Africa vary by location and season. Historically, the prices of food and beverage commodities have increased materially during El Niño episodes, as extreme weather conditions hinder production (figure 13.B). In the current episode, notable effects are expected in cocoa, palm oil, rice, and sugar markets, although annual average prices are forecast to increase significantly only for palm oil and rice.

results.text: FERTILIZERSCOMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 39 Recent developments Nitrogen (urea) prices averaged $399/mt in 2026Q3, down 42 percent (q/q) and 18 percent (y/y), after peaking at $857/mt in April (figure 18.A). Prices eased further in the first half of October. The initial retreat during 2026Q2 reflected China’s easing of export restrictions in May, the temporary reduction in hostilities following the June memorandum of understand- ing between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran, and reductions in purchases, partly owing to the end of spring planting in the Northern Hemisphere. Increased exports from China and other major suppliers, including Egypt, Nigeria, and Oman, helped sustain a return to more normal price levels. China’s urea exports are expected to reach 7.0 million metric tons (mmt) in 2026, up from 4.9 mmt in 2025.

Urea prices are forecast to fall by 16 percent in 2027 and 14 percent in 2028, assuming Middle Eastern exports recover, natural gas prices ease, Fertilizers The World Bank Group’s fertilizer price index fell by 22 percent in 2026Q3 (q/q) and continued to decline in October, fully reversing the 2026Q2 surge that followed the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Urea prices drove both swings, while other fertilizer prices rose less sharply but remained elevated in 2026Q3. Despite the recent retreat, the index is projected to rise by about 14 percent in 2026 (y/y), reflecting shipping disruptions in the Middle East, associated increases in input costs, and trade restrictions. Prices are forecast to fall by 12 percent in 2027 and a further 8 percent in 2028 as input costs ease and supplies recover, aided by increased exports from producers outside the Gulf region.

Upside risks to the outlook for urea prices include an escalation in the Middle East conflict that raises input costs, particularly for natural gas, above baseline expectations. More specifically, continued conflict could lead to an extension of Qatar’s force majeure, imposed in March, on contracts to sell LNG and related products, including urea. Export restrictions by major producers are another potential source of renewed price surges. Conversely, a swift reduction of geopolitical tensions in the Gulf region could lead to a surge of exports, materially lowering prices, although infrastructure damage is likely to delay the full recovery of urea production. After a projected 7 percent increase in 2026, DAP prices are forecast to drop by about 18 percent in 2027 and 17 percent in 2028.

results.text: Most commodity analysis appropriately focuses on the supply and demand fundamentals of individual markets. While that approach remains important, it provides only a partial view when volatility associated with one commodity is linked to developments in other commodity markets. This Special Focus examines price volatility connectedness across 15 internationally traded commodities in six groups—energy, food, industrial metals, livestock, precious metals, and soft commodities (such as coffee and cotton)— using daily data from 2006 to 2026. Price volatility connectedness measures how much of the variance in a commodity’s price volatility can be explained by shocks affecting prices in other commodity markets.

SPECIAL FOCUS COMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 48 Introduction Commodity prices often move in tandem because many markets are exposed to common shifts in global activity, input costs, trade, and financial conditions. For instance, a slowdown in industrial activity can weaken demand for energy and industrial metals at the same time, while disruptions to energy supply can raise transport and fertilizer costs and spill into agricultural markets. Periods of financial or geopolitical stress can broaden these movements across otherwise distinct commodity groups (World Bank 2024). Understanding these linkages is key because commodity price shocks affect inflation, fiscal revenues, trade balances, and food and energy security, particularly in emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) with large commodity exposures (Balcilar, Usman and Agan 2024; World Bank 2026a).

SPECIAL FOCUSCOMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 49 six groups: energy, food, industrial metals, livestock, precious metals, and soft commodities. The products include crude oil and U.S. natural gas in the energy group; aluminum, copper, nickel, and zinc in the industrial metals group; maize, soybeans, and wheat in the food group; live cattle and lean hogs in the livestock group; gold and silver in the precious metals group; and coffee and cotton in the soft commodities group.3 The common sample spans May 5, 2006, the earliest date for which data are available, to June 26, 2026. Price volatility is measured using the range-based estimator of Garman and Klass (1980), which combines daily opening, closing, high, and low prices. T o capture relationships across a relatively large number of markets, the analysis estimates an elastic net vector autoregression model (appendix SF .1).
